summary: TRILL provides least-cost forwarding in networks of arbitrary topology without configuration. This document specifies ESADI, a protocol that lets TRILL switches share end station address information, optionally on a per-VLAN or per-fine-grained-label basis.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL switches normally work out where a device is attached by watching the frames they forward. ESADI lets a switch instead announce the addresses of the devices plugged into it, so other switches learn about a move straight away rather than waiting for the old record to expire.

subtitle: Lets TRILL switches share which end stations are attached where.

tldr.problem: A TRILL switch normally learns which end station is attached to it by watching the traffic it forwards, so a move between switches can black-hole frames for tens of seconds while the old information ages out.
tldr.mechanism: ESADI is an optional protocol, run per VLAN or fine-grained label, in which switches announce the MAC addresses of their attached end stations, with a confidence rating and optional authentication, using a modified form of the IS-IS reliable flooding mechanism.
tldr.outcome: Switches learn about attachments faster and can authenticate them, and the information is only flooded to the switches taking part in that label. The document replaces the ESADI description in RFC 6325 and is not backwards compatible with it.

facts.label: Maximum fragment zero payload
facts.value: 1446 bytes with an Inner.VLAN, 1442 with an Inner.FGL

today: RFC 7357 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6325, replacing its ESADI description, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the PDUs defined in RFC 7356.

sections.title: Why a Second Way to Learn Addresses
sections.content:
The TRILL protocol provides least-cost pairwise data forwarding without configuration in multi-hop networks with arbitrary topologies, safe forwarding even during temporary loops, and multipathing for both unicast and multicast traffic. It uses the IS-IS link-state routing protocol with a header that carries a hop count, and it supports two kinds of data labeling: VLANs and fine-grained labels (FGLs). Devices that implement TRILL are called TRILL switches or RBridges.

There are five ways a TRILL switch can learn end station addresses. One of them is ESADI, an optional, Data Label scoped way for switches to tell each other about end station addresses and which switch they are attached to. A switch taking part in ESADI for a label may announce the addresses of some, all or none of its attached end stations in that label.

By default, switches with attached end stations learn addresses from the data plane as they ingress and egress native frames, although that learning can be turned off. ESADI has two claimed advantages over that. The first is security: a switch can announce end stations that were enrolled with an authenticated registration, for example using a cryptographically based Extensible Authentication Protocol method over IEEE 802.1X, and ESADI can authenticate its own message payloads so that tampering with them in transit is very difficult. The second is speed: ESADI updates MAC addresses and their point of attachment quickly. If an end station is unplugged from one switch and plugged into another, frames destined for its MAC address can be black-holed, because they still go to the older egress switch until the cached information at some remote ingress switch times out, which can take tens of seconds.

MAC address reachability, some ESADI parameters and optional authentication information travel in ESADI packets rather than in the TRILL IS-IS protocol. For each Data Label, ESADI is a logical overlay on the TRILL topology, and an advantage of that arrangement is that the attachment information is not flooded to every TRILL switch, but only to those advertising ESADI participation for the label where those end stations appear.
sections.plainLanguage: Watching traffic tells a switch where a device is, but only after the device sends something. ESADI lets a switch say so directly, which is both quicker and easier to authenticate.

sections.title: How ESADI Is Built on IS-IS
sections.content:
ESADI is a Data Label scoped way for TRILL switches to announce and learn end station addresses quickly and securely. A switch announcing participation in ESADI for one or more labels is an ESADI RBridge.

ESADI is optional and separate from the mandatory TRILL IS-IS that every RBridge in a campus runs. There is a separate ESADI instance for each Data Label, and for each such label there is, in effect, a modified instance of the IS-IS reliable flooding mechanism in which ESADI RBridges may choose to take part. Several instances may share implementation components inside a switch, as long as each still operates independently, so the link state database could be one database with a field naming the label each record applies to, or a separate database per label. The update process runs separately for each instance and independently of the TRILL IS-IS update process.

ESADI does no routing calculations, so there is no reason for pseudonodes and none are created. A relatively large amount of ESADI data has to be distributed in some circumstances, which would need many LSP fragments, so the ESADI-LSP, ESADI-CSNP and ESADI-PSNP payloads are formatted as Extended Level 1 Circuit Scope PDUs, which allows up to 2**16 fragments.

After the TRILL header, an ESADI packet has an inner Ethernet header whose Inner.MacDA is All-Egress-RBridges, an inner Data Label naming the VLAN or FGL of interest, and the L2-IS-IS Ethertype followed by the ESADI payload. The outer destination address is the All-RBridges multicast address for a multicast PDU, or the unicast address of the next-hop RBridge for a unicast PDU. The V and R fields are zero and the M bit is one, unless the PDU was unicast. The Origin RBridge MAC address must be unique across the campus, and each ESADI RBridge must use the same Inner.MacSA for every ESADI packet it originates.
sections.plainLanguage: ESADI reuses the link-state flooding machinery of IS-IS, but runs a separate copy of it for each VLAN or label, and only for the switches that opt in. Its packets travel through the TRILL network as ordinary TRILL data frames.

sections.title: What an ESADI Packet Carries
sections.content:
The ESADI payloads are structured like the IS-IS Extended Level 1 Circuit Scope LSP, CSNP and PSNP PDUs, except where noted, and are always TRILL encapsulated on the wire as if they were TRILL data packets. The information distributed includes a list of local end station MAC addresses connected to the originating RBridge and, for each address, a one octet unsigned confidence rating in the range 0 to 254. It is up to the originating RBridge which locally connected MAC addresses it advertises and with what confidence; it may advertise all, some or none. Some ESADI parameters of the advertising RBridge and, optionally, authentication information are included as well.

ESADI-LSPs MUST NOT contain a Data Label ID in their payload, because the label the data applies to is the label of the enclosing TRILL data packet. A Data Label ID inside the payload would clash with that and with any future label mapping scheme, so any such field in an ESADI-LSP MUST be ignored.

Neighbour determination needs no Hellos. The ESADI instance for a label at one switch works out its ESADI neighbours by examining the TRILL IS-IS link state database for switches that are data reachable from it and that are announcing participation in that label's ESADI. A switch that becomes data unreachable, or whose entries are purged, is lost as a neighbour and dropped from every ESADI instance. When it stops announcing participation it ceases to be a neighbour for that label's instances. A participation announcement for a VLAN scoped instance is a flag bit in the Interested VLANs sub-TLV, and for an FGL scoped instance a flag bit in the Interested Labels sub-TLV.

Only three PDUs are used: the ESADI-LSP, ESADI-CSNP and ESADI-PSNP. There are no Hello or MTU PDUs, because ESADI builds no topology, does no routing calculations and does not determine the MTU; it uses the distribution trees and the campus minimum link MTU determined by the core TRILL IS-IS.
sections.plainLanguage: Each announcement lists the MAC addresses attached to one switch, with a confidence number for each. The protocol has no handshake at all: switches work out who is taking part from the ordinary TRILL link state database.

sections.title: Electing the Designated RBridge
sections.content:
Because ESADI announces no adjacency and performs no routing, the ESADI designated RBridge (DRB) never creates a pseudonode. A DRB is still needed to issue ESADI-CSNP PDUs and to answer ESADI-PSNP PDUs for LSP synchronisation.

The election works much like the DRB election on a TRILL IS-IS broadcast link, with two differences. The candidates are the local ESADI instance for the label and all remote ESADI instances at switches that are data reachable from the electing switch and that announce in their TRILL IS-IS LSP that they take part in ESADI for that label. The winner is the instance with the highest priority field, which is seven bits wide, with ties broken by the System ID, comparing the fields as unsigned integers so that the larger magnitude is the higher priority. Unlike the broadcast case, the SNPA or MAC address is not considered in the tiebreak, and there is no Port ID.
sections.plainLanguage: One switch takes the job of keeping everyone's link state in step, the same job a designated router does on an ordinary IS-IS link. It is the switch with the highest configured priority, with the System ID breaking ties.

sections.title: Flooding, Unicast and Timing
sections.content:
Following the usual IS-IS rules, an ESADI instance sends nothing when it has no ESADI adjacencies. The MTU available to an ESADI payload is at least 24 bytes less than for TRILL IS-IS, because of the extra fields needed, so the inner ESADI payload MUST NOT exceed Sz minus 24 for a VLAN instance or Sz minus 28 for an FGL instance; a larger payload that arrives is still processed normally. The priority bit that marks an LSP fragment for high priority flooding SHOULD be set on ESADI-LSP fragment zero, because it matters that the ESADI parameter sub-TLV gets through promptly, and SHOULD NOT be set on other fragments.

Unicast is optional. On what looks like a multi-access link to an ESADI instance there is really a set of multi-hop distribution trees, so sending a multicast frame on one can cost far more than sending a unicast frame. ESADI PDUs MAY therefore be TRILL unicast if it is confirmed that the destination RBridge supports receiving them, which the recipient signals with a flag in its ESADI parameter data. In a unicast ESADI packet the outer destination address is the unicast address of the next-hop RBridge, and in the TRILL header the M bit is zero and the egress nickname is the nickname of the destination RBridge.

The reliable flooding mechanism is modified in a few ways. When an instance sees a new neighbour, its self-originated LSP fragments are scheduled to be sent and may be unicast to that neighbour if it advertises unicast support. Because every other instance for the same label would do the same at the same moment, there could be a surge of traffic to the new neighbour, so the instances SHOULD wait an interval before sending. One suggested interval is a random value based on the RBridge's nickname, such as 2000 times the nickname divided by 2**16 milliseconds.

Because the multi-hop distribution tree with Reverse Path Forwarding Check used for multicast distribution is typically less reliable than a single local broadcast hop, an ESADI RBridge SHOULD also transmit an ESADI-CSNP for an instance if it sees one or more neighbours for that instance, does not believe it is the DRB, and has neither received nor sent an ESADI-CSNP for the instance for the average of the DRB's CSNP Time and its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Announcements are flooded like link state updates, and the protocol adds small delays so that a new switch joining does not receive a flood of traffic at once, and so that the announcements survive the multi-hop tree.

sections.title: What an ESADI-LSP Contains
sections.content:
The contents of an ESADI-LSP are zero or more MAC-Reachability TLVs, optionally an Authentication TLV, and exactly one ESADI parameter APPsub-TLV. Because these PDUs use the extended format, the Type and Length fields in the TLVs are 16 bits wide. For robustness, the payload of an ESADI-LSP number zero, and of any ESADI-CSNP or ESADI-PSNP covering fragment zero, MUST NOT exceed 1470 minus 24 bytes, which is 1446 bytes, when it has an Inner.VLAN, or 1470 minus 28 bytes, which is 1442 bytes, when it has an Inner.FGL. A longer one received is still processed normally.

The ESADI parameter APPsub-TLV MUST be included in a TRILL GENINFO TLV in ESADI-LSP number zero. If it is missing, or if that LSP is not known, the sender's priority defaults to 0x40 and the CSNP Time defaults to 30. If there is more than one occurrence, the first is used, and occurrences in non-zero fragments are ignored. The sub-TLV has a Type of ESADI-PARAM, which is TRILL APPsub-TLV type 0x0001, a variable Length with a minimum of 3, a reserved bit that must be sent as zero, the seven bit priority, the CSNP Time as an unsigned number of seconds, and a byte of flags. The CSNP Time is the period during which the originating RBridge, if it is the DRB, will send at least three ESADI-CSNP PDUs. The UN flag says that the originating RBridge will accept and process ESADI PDUs sent by TRILL unicast; the remaining flag bits are reserved.

The MAC-Reachability TLVs, specified in RFC 6165, hold one or more unicast MAC addresses of end stations that are both on a port and in a VLAN for which the originating RBridge is Appointed Forwarder, together with the one octet unsigned confidence value in the range 0 to 254. A received confidence of 255 is treated as 254, so that received address information can still be overridden by local address information configured with a confidence of 255. The TLVs in TRILL ESADI PDUs must not contain the Data Label ID; only the Inner.VLAN or Inner.FGL tag says which label the LSP applies to.
sections.plainLanguage: Each announcement holds the list of attached MAC addresses with a confidence number for each, plus a small block of settings that tell other switches how this switch wants to be treated.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of the Announcements
sections.content:
ESADI PDUs can be authenticated with the Authentication TLV of RFC 5310. The default follows the state of TRILL IS-IS shared secret authentication for TRILL IS-IS LSP PDUs: if a switch has TRILL IS-IS authentication in effect, ESADI PDUs from it MUST use the same algorithm unless configured otherwise, and the ESADI keying material is derived from the IS-IS LSP shared key by HMAC-SHA256 over the 11 byte ASCII string TRILL ESADI and the shared key. If TRILL IS-IS authentication is not in effect, ESADI PDUs from that switch are unsecured by default. Manually configured ESADI authentication is not restricted by the TRILL IS-IS security configuration.

The reachability that ESADI announces is sometimes an authenticated registration, and combining that with authentication of the ESADI PDUs makes the reachability information substantially more trustworthy than what is learned by watching the data plane. Even so, ESADI means trusting every other RBridge in the campus that holds the keying material needed to build a valid Authentication TLV. There may be no need to authenticate ESADI PDUs where that threat does not exist, for example on inter-RBridge trunks in a campus with secure RBridges, even when some end stations are attached over wireless links that use their own authentication.

On privacy, the reachability information distributed by ESADI has substantial privacy implications in many but not all circumstances. In a campus with independent user end stations at the edge, the MAC addresses could uniquely identify the people using them, and their reachability is sensitive information, particularly if it is logged. At an Internet Exchange Point, the addresses advertised would typically be those of the service providers' router ports, where there would be few privacy concerns. Records that include a modest history can be useful for managing a network and troubleshooting, and may in some cases be required by law or for billing. Operators should balance these considerations for their own network and should not keep logs of MAC reachability information longer than is clearly required.
sections.plainLanguage: The announcements can be signed, and by default follow whatever authentication the network already uses for its link state. But the list of who is connected can be sensitive, so it is worth keeping no more history than the network really needs.

sections.title: What This Document Changes in RFC 6325
sections.content:
This document replaces the description of the TRILL ESADI protocol in Section 4.2.5 of RFC 6325, including all of its subsections, gives more detail on ESADI, updates other ESADI related sections of RFC 6325, and prevails over RFC 6325 wherever they conflict. Familiarity with RFC 6325 is therefore assumed.

One change is not backwards compatible: the format of the ESADI link state PDUs. The reason given is the substantially greater amount of information that can now be carried, and the very limited, if any, deployment of the RFC 6325 version of ESADI. The format of the ESADI-LSP, CSNP and PSNP payloads moves from the IS-IS Level 1 format to the Extended Level 1 Circuit Scope format, whose information carrying capacity is 256 times greater, and the PDU numbers change from 18, 24 and 26 to 10, 11 and 12 so that a PDU cannot be mis-parsed. Implementations of the two versions therefore discard each other's PDUs, and information distributed by one kind of implementation reaches only implementations of the same kind.

Unicast support is optional and backwards compatible, because it is used only when the recipient RBridge signals its support. The timing changes add staggered delay for non-originators of ESADI-LSP fragments that are asked for by CSNP and PSNP messages, and suggest staggered timing of unicast ESADI-LSPs when a new RBridge appears on the virtual link. Both are about congestion, and a lost message is later retransmitted as part of the robust flooding mechanism.

Handling of the persistent reachability of the same MAC address within the same Data Label from two or more RBridges is substantially modified, with explicit replacement of some text in Section 4.2.6 of RFC 6325. A mixed campus is not a problem for that condition; the more implementations follow the improved behaviour, the better the traffic spreading and the less likely the address flip-flopping problem. A smooth incremental migration is possible because RBridges can use the mandatory, enabled by default data plane address learning alongside ESADI, which fills the gaps left by the two versions not talking to each other, though without the speed or security advantages of ESADI.
sections.plainLanguage: This document replaces the ESADI description in the base TRILL specification, and the replacement does not work with the old one. Switches running the two versions will ignore each other's announcements, so a network has to run one version throughout.
